title: Does Reciting the Name Guarantee Rebirth?
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Master Shandao says: “Precisely because reciting the name is easy, continuity brings birth. If one can keep thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment, then out of ten, ten are born; out of a hundred, a hundred are born. ......

inline.s: Master Shandao says: “Precisely because reciting the name is easy, continuity brings birth. If one can keep thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment, then out of ten, ten are born; out of a hundred, a hundred are born. ......

May all people consider this well for themselves: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night. When the final thought ends this life, the very next thought is birth. To receive forever the unconditioned joy of the Dharma, until attaining Buddhahood — is that not the greatest delight?”

[Precisely because reciting the name is easy] Precisely because reciting the Buddha’s name is easier to accomplish than visualizing the Buddha. [Continuity brings birth] At the hour of death, as long as the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is continuous (uninterrupted by deluded thoughts), one attains birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. [With lifelong commitment] One who carries out this practice throughout life. [Stir the mind and discipline oneself] To stir the mind is to spur one’s mind to do what should be done; to discipline oneself is to restrain oneself from doing what should not be done. The four characters “li xin ke ji” are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and clearing away obstacles. [Never ceasing day or night] Never ceasing, day or night, the unbroken succession of thoughts.
The Original Vow school has two great falsehoods: one is the “Hongan Gate,” the other is “reciting the name guarantees birth” — and it claims these are the core of Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought.

For example, in the Pure Land master Jingzong’s forty-three-episode lecture series “Master Shandao’s Pure Land Thought,” the whole message boils down to the claim that “the Hongan Gate and reciting the name guaranteeing birth are the core of Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought.” But what are the facts? The fact is: Master Shandao never spoke of the Hongan Gate at all — this was entirely fabricated by Hōnen (see
Hōnen Fabricated the Hongan Gate
). Nor did Master Shandao ever say that reciting the name guarantees birth. On the contrary, Master Shandao said:
“Continuity brings birth
(see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
“birth through right mindfulness at life’s end”
(see
Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death

The “Hongan Gate” and “reciting the name guarantees birth” — which they themselves fabricated — they then foist upon Master Shandao, falsely claiming this is his Pure Land thought. Is this how one follows Master Shandao (Hōnen, Master Huijing, Master Jingzong, and the rest never stop proclaiming that they follow Master Shandao)? Is this how one promotes Master Shandao’s Pure Land thought?
A visitor came with the Original Vow school’s book, Shandao’s Explanation of the Eighteenth Vow, and challenged me, saying:

Concerning the Eighteenth Vow (the Original Vow), the root of the Pure Land school, Master Shandao, a manifestation of Amitābha, has a very concise explanation (called the “texts conveying the meaning of the Original Vow”):
Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra, the “text conveying the meaning of the Original Vow,”
says
If, when I attain Buddhahood, the beings of the ten directions who call my name and wish to be born in my land,
down to ten thoughts
, should fail to be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Master Shandao’s Dharma Gate of Contemplation, the “text conveying the meaning of the Original Vow,”
says
If, when I become a Buddha, the beings of the ten directions who wish to be born in my land and call my name,
down to ten utterances
, relying on the power of my vow, should fail to be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
Master Shandao’s Liturgy for Birth in the Pure Land, the “text conveying the meaning of the Original Vow,”
says
If, when I become a Buddha, the beings of the ten directions who call my name,
down to ten utterances

, should fail to be born, may I not attain perfect enlightenment; that Buddha has now appeared and attained Buddhahood in this world, so you should know that his original vow, his weighty vow, is not in vain: beings who call and remember him will surely attain birth.

In these three “texts conveying the meaning of the Original Vow,” it is said that “down to ten thoughts” or “down to ten utterances” ensures birth. That is to say: as long as one recites the Buddha’s name ten times with a scattered mind in ordinary times, one is certain to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at death. Therefore, Master Shandao said: reciting the name guarantees birth. Is this not so?
To this, I reply as follows:

The ancients prized brevity in writing (this also gave non-Buddhist heresies such as the Original Vow school the opportunity to quote out of context and thereby distort and tamper with the Buddhist teachings). Therefore, when interpreting, one must always read the preceding and following passages,
as well as the author’s overall thought,
together, and never take a phrase literally in isolation or quote out of context.
In the time of Master Shandao (
), the influence of his teacher, Master Daochuo (
), was immense. Through a series of teachings by Master Daochuo (
see
Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching
the understanding that “down to ten thoughts” in the Eighteenth Vow
refers to ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end
had become an undisputed consensus.
For example,
Master Daochuo said:
If there are beings who, though they have spent a whole life committing evil,
at the hour of death keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession,
and call my name — if they are not born, I will not attain perfect enlightenment.”
(from the Anle Ji)
Therefore, whenever the phrases “down to ten thoughts” or “down to ten utterances” are mentioned,
everyone knows they refer to ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end
, so no further words were added in the writing. For example, in Master Daochuo’s own teachings there are such passages. Master Daochuo’s Anle Ji says:
“From the utmost of a whole life,
down to ten thoughts
, all without exception attain birth. Upon reaching that land, one enters the assembly of the definitely settled, equal in merit to ten thousand kalpas of practice on this path.”
Before this “from the utmost of a whole life down to ten thoughts, all without exception attain birth,” Master Daochuo has already clearly stated:
at the hour of death, ten thoughts in unbroken succession
calling my name — if they are not born, I will not attain perfect enlightenment.”

Therefore, reading the preceding and following passages together, “down to ten thoughts” means ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end, not ten scattered recitations of the Buddha’s name in ordinary times.
(Note: On the immensity of Master Daochuo’s influence at that time, see
Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching
. Moreover, Master Shandao himself settled his mind on the Pure Land under Master Daochuo’s influence. See
Biography of Master Shandao (Vernacular and Original)
Concerning the meaning of the Eighteenth Vow, Master Daochuo has already made it very clear in the Anle Ji:
If there are beings who, though they have spent a whole life committing evil,
at the hour of death keep ten thoughts in unbroken succession,
and call my name — if they are not born, I will not attain perfect enlightenment.”
Here Master Daochuo gives a precise explanation of the meaning of “down to ten thoughts” in the Eighteenth Vow:
at the hour of death, ten thoughts in unbroken succession.
Moreover, Master Daochuo gave a series of important teachings on “ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end” (see
The Eighteenth Vow
Moreover, Master Shandao himself clearly stated how one can attain birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss:
continuity brings birth.
Master Shandao said:
“Precisely because reciting the name is easy
(precisely because reciting the name is easier than visualization)
continuity brings birth
If one can keep thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment
(one who carries out this practice throughout life)
, then out of ten, ten are born; out of a hundred, a hundred are born.
May all people consider this well for themselves,
in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down,
you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night

If Master Shandao advocated “reciting the name guarantees birth,” why did he also say “thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment” and “in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night”?
Moreover, Master Shandao specially wrote the Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death to emphasize
birth through right mindfulness at life’s end
(see
Master Shandao’s Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death
Since the Original Vow school claims to follow Master Shandao, why do you not follow Master Shandao’s teaching of “
thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment
” and “
in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night
”? Instead you tout “there is no need to practice.” Is there truly no need to practice? Read carefully Master Shandao’s teachings!
(see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao: Continuity Brings Rebirth

[Stir the mind and discipline oneself] To stir the mind is to spur one’s mind to do what should be done; to discipline oneself is to restrain oneself from doing what should not be done. The four characters “li xin ke ji” are a powerful weapon for overcoming difficulties and clearing away obstacles — to spur oneself and restrain oneself. “Discipline oneself”: to restrain oneself. [When the final thought ends this life, the very next thought is birth] This means: because the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name is continuous, the very last thought at life’s end is certain to be the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name, and immediately after that last thought one is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The Original Vow school, disregarding these facts, twists Master Shandao’s “down to ten thoughts” and “down to ten utterances” into ten scattered recitations of the Buddha’s name in ordinary times, and from this concludes that Master Shandao said reciting the name guarantees birth. But in fact, what Master Shandao plainly taught was
“continuity brings birth”
and
“birth through right mindfulness at life’s end”

. How can one so recklessly distort in disregard of the facts? To study Buddhism, one must act from a truthful heart. As the saying goes: “To cover one’s eyes and catch sparrows is to deceive oneself.” If even so small a thing cannot be accomplished through self-deception, how much less the great matter of birth and death!

[Cover one’s eyes and catch sparrows] To cover one’s eyes while catching sparrows, supposing they cannot see you — a metaphor for deceiving oneself. [If even so small a thing cannot be accomplished through self-deception, how much less the great matter of birth and death] If even so small a thing as catching sparrows cannot be accomplished through self-deception, how could the great matter of liberation from birth and death possibly be accomplished through self-deception? [Self-deception] To deceive oneself. The Original Vow school deceives itself, supposing that by rewriting Master Shandao’s teaching of “continuity brings birth” into “reciting the name guarantees birth,” one may recite the Buddha’s name with a scattered mind in ordinary times and then be certain of birth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss at death.
To distinguish true from false, I suggest readers carefully read
Master Daochuo’s Pure Land Teaching
and
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

, and compare them with the Original Vow school’s touted claim of “reciting the name guarantees birth”; then truth and falsehood will be clear at a glance. This is a matter of the utmost importance, bearing directly on whether one attains birth — on no account take it lightly!
Examples of “the ancients prized brevity in writing” abound in the sutras and treatises. For instance, Master Ouyi says in his Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra:

“Now in the Pure Land, even those who committed the five grave offenses and the ten evils, who accomplished ten thoughts and were born carrying their karma, dwelling in the lowest grade of the lowest birth, all attain the three kinds of non-retrogression.”
Based on the context
(see
Commentary on the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra

, it is clear that this passage means: to attain these three stages of non-retrogression (non-retrogression of position, of practice, and of mindfulness) in this Sahā world is extremely difficult; a bodhisattva must practice for a great asaṃkhyeya kalpa before he can realize this stage (avaivartika). But beings who have committed the five grave offenses and the ten evils, as long as they accomplish ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end and are born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, immediately realize these three stages of non-retrogression. The Amitābha Sutra says:
“In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all beings who are born there are avaivartika.”
Here “accomplished ten thoughts” is a shortened form of “
accomplished ten unbroken thoughts at life’s end
”; this is already the consensus of Pure Land students, so the patriarchs and great masters, in their writing, briefly say “accomplished ten thoughts.”

If one follows the Original Vow school’s method of quoting out of context, one could conclude: Master Ouyi said that a person of the five grave offenses and ten evils, as long as he recites the Buddha’s name ten times in ordinary times, can realize the three stages of non-retrogression.
Another example: there is this passage in the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra:

Question: Since ten thoughts or even one thought suffices for birth, why the need for seven days? Answer: Without the seven days of practice in ordinary times, how could there be ten thoughts or one thought at life’s end?
The meaning of this passage is:
The student further asks: since ten thoughts or one thought
in unbroken succession

at life’s end can bring birth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, why is there any need for the practice of single-minded, undistracted recitation of the Buddha’s name? Answer: Without the ordinary-time practice of single-minded, undistracted recitation, how could there be ten thoughts or one thought
in unbroken succession
at life’s end?

If one does not interpret this passage according to its context in the Essential Explanation of the Amitābha Sutra, one could again conclude: Master Ouyi said that one need only recite the Buddha’s name for seven days in ordinary times to achieve ten thoughts or one thought at life’s end. Little does one realize that, seen in the context of the whole work, “the seven days of practice in ordinary times” refers to the ordinary-time practice of single-minded, undistracted recitation. (The Amitābha Sutra says:
“Hold fast to the name, whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, single-mindedly and without distraction, ......”

Another example: the Original Vow school, disregarding the sutra’s meaning, quotes out of context and twists the “down to ten thoughts” of the Eighteenth Vow into ten scattered recitations of the Buddha’s name in ordinary times, and so says: reciting the name guarantees birth; there is no need to practice, no need to keep precepts, no need to do good, no need to purify one’s mind, and even a whole life of evil makes no difference. But what are the facts? Amitābha Buddha’s Eighteenth Vow was proclaimed by Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sutra of the Buddha of Infinite Life, and in that very sutra the World-Honored One exhorts:
“Be upright in body and correct in conduct, and do all manner of good; cultivate yourself and purify your body, wash away the defilements of the mind.
Though one toils through one lifetime, in the space of an instant one will be born in the land of the Buddha of Infinite Life, where joy is boundless.”
And at the end of the sutra, the World-Honored One earnestly enjoins:
“You should believe and accord, and practice according to the Dharma.”
If “reciting the name guarantees birth,” why did the World-Honored One still speak of
“washing away the defilements of the mind”
and
“though one toils through one lifetime”
, and still speak of
“practicing according to the Dharma”

? The Original Vow school has not only failed to believe and accord with the Buddha’s teaching but has done the very opposite! What result can there be from thus deceiving oneself and others? (On the correct meaning of “down to ten thoughts,” see
The Eighteenth Vow
Master Shandao is Amitābha Buddha returned, and his teachings are equivalent to words spoken by Amitābha Buddha himself. Master Shandao teaches:
“If one can keep thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment, then out of ten, ten are born; out of a hundred, a hundred are born.
May all people consider this well for themselves: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night.”
Why do you not follow and practice according to these teachings? Why instead heed the false doctrines of Hōnen, Shinran, and the like, cutting off your own wisdom-life?
Master Shandao, who is Amitābha Buddha returned, teaches:
Continuity brings birth

. If one can keep thought following thought in unbroken succession, with lifelong commitment, then out of ten, ten are born; out of a hundred, a hundred are born. ...... May all people consider this well for themselves: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, you must stir your mind and discipline yourself, never ceasing day or night.”
Our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, after proclaiming the forty-eight vows in the Sutra of the Buddha of Infinite Life, further taught:
“You should believe and accord,
and practice according to the Dharma
Uphold the sutras and precepts
, receive and practice the Way of the Dharma, without transgression or omission.’ ‘
Be upright in body
and do all manner of good
cultivate yourself and purify your body
wash away the defilements of the mind
. ...... Though one toils through one lifetime, in the space of an instant one will be born in the land of the Buddha of Infinite Life, where joy is boundless.”

But the Original Vow school touts: reciting the name guarantees birth; there is no need to practice, no need to keep precepts, no need to do good, no need to purify one’s mind, and even a whole life of evil makes no difference (this is the Original Vow school’s “theory of the evil person as the true object,” see
The Original Vow School Is a Non-Buddhist Heresy
the article
). Setting the two side by side, one can see clearly:
the Original Vow school is a complete and utter inversion of the teaching!
It works directly against the Buddha, point for point!

As a disciple of the Buddha, why do you not listen to the words of Master Shandao, the manifestation of Amitābha, nor to the words of our teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, but instead allow yourself to be deluded by the Original Vow school and run after them? Do you know how grave the consequences of this are? (On the consequences, see
The Original Vow School Is a Non-Buddhist Heresy
the article
The purpose of studying the sutras and treatises is to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so as to guide one’s own practice. If the causal ground is not genuine, the result will be crooked.

Therefore, when reading the sutras and treatises, on no account take phrases literally in isolation or quote out of context. And quoting out of context with ulterior motives harms others and harms oneself. (Why bring such suffering upon oneself!)
The Original Vow school inverts the teaching, its aim being to distort and tamper with the Buddhist doctrines so as to destroy the Buddha’s true Dharma
see
The Original Vow School Is a Non-Buddhist Heresy
the article

. The error of inverting the teaching is perfectly obvious; so how do they deceive the faithful? Their method is to quote out of context and distort the sutras and treatises! The founding patriarch of the Original Vow school, Hōnen, built his career precisely on quoting out of context and distorting the sutras and treatises
(see
Hōnen Fabricated the Hongan Gate
and
Hōnen Distorts the Sutra of Praise of the Pure Land
, and he made this the school’s supreme skill, handed down from generation to generation.
